title: Every thing has its end; whatever acts tends to some good; intelligent and non-intelligent agents
pass_a_gloss: Pass A clause gloss: comparing them with one another plus ordering these to that same end, while those that same which do not understand stand as moved rather by natural inclination — yet both act toward an end, or, to speak more clearly, tend into an end — although there stands as a difference — that same those that same which understand move themselves to the end plus act by knowing the end plus the means. 3. since that same cannot be an end that same which has no account belonging toward good. Whatever acts, whether it works with cognition or without cognition properly so called, operates toward an end, plus therefore tends to some good: 2. Proverbs 16:4). but all things stand as toward an end (Genesis 1:31; — because neither God nor nature does or produces anything in vain. its own good, plus its own perfection: — for among all the saints — indeed among the sane — it stands as confessed that same to each thing some end belonging toward its own belongs.
pass_b_english: For among all the saints — indeed among the sane — it is confessed that to each thing some end of its own belongs, its own good, and its own perfection: because neither God nor nature does or produces anything in vain, but all things are for an end ([[Genesis 1:31>>Gen. 1:31]]; [[Proverbs 16:4>>Prov. 16:4]]).

2. Whatever acts, whether it works with cognition or without cognition properly so called, operates for an end, and therefore tends to some good: since that cannot be an end which has no account of good.

3. Although there is a difference — that those which understand move themselves to the end and act by knowing the end and the means, comparing them with one another and ordering these to that end, while those which do not understand are moved rather by natural inclination — yet both act for an end, or, to speak more clearly, tend into an end.
source_text: Nam apud omnes sanctos, imo sanos in confesso est: unicuique rei suum quendam finem convenire, suum bonum, suamque perfectionem: quia nec Deus, neque natura quicquam frustra faciunt aut producunt, sed omnia propter finem, Gen. 1.v.31. Prov. 16.v.4. 2. Quicquid agit, sive cum cognitione id operetur, sive absque cognitione proprie dicta, id omne operatur propter finem, atque adeo ad aliquod bonum tendit: cum finis esse nequeat, quod boni rationem non habet. 3. Quamvis discrimen sit, quod, quae intelligunt, semetipsa in finem moveant, & agant cognoscendo finem & media, interque sese conferendo, & haec ad illum ordinando; quae vero non intelligunt, moveantur potius per naturalem inclinationem: utraque tamen agunt propter finem, seu, ut clarius dicam, in finem tendunt.
